summary: This object is a (111)-oriented monocrystalline Fe-16 at.%Al (Fe-16%Al) specimen grown by the Bridgman method and then given an intermediate-temperature anneal of 300 °C for 3 days in high-purity argon. It is one condition within a series of 300 °C anneals of different durations used by Herrmann, Inden and Sauthoff to probe how the state of atomic (short-range) order influences the low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys. The central question addressed with this specimen is whether the ordering reactions occurring below 600 °C in the K-state composition range manifest themselves in the mechanical response; the answer, from its universal hardness of ≈2000 N/mm² being equal to that of the as-grown monocrystal, is that short-range order has only a minor effect.
composition: Binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal Al content of 16 at.% (16.0 at.% real, i.e. 8.4 wt.-%), the balance being Fe of 99.99% purity (zone-melted to minimise impurities). Al is the sole deliberate alloying addition, with 99.999% purity; its purpose is solid-solution hardening of the bcc iron matrix together with reduced density and improved oxidation and high-temperature corrosion resistance. The unavoidable impurity content is deliberately low: C 45 wt.ppm, Si 40 wt.ppm and O 60 wt.ppm for this monocrystal, keeping carbon well below 100 wt.ppm so that carbide formation and the carbon-related embrittlement reported in earlier Fe-Al studies are avoided.
processing: The specimen originates from binary Fe-Al melted by vacuum induction in Al2O3 crucibles and solidified in Cu moulds, from which (111)-oriented monocrystals up to 10 cm long were grown by the Bridgman method at a 10–15 mm/h pulling rate, crystal growth with subsequent cooling taking about 12 h overall. The monocrystals were etched in ammonium persulfate and oriented by a laser light-figure method. Test pieces were then cut by electrostatic discharge machining and mechanically polished; the monocrystals were not given an ultrasonic acetone clean. The dedicated heat treatment of this object is an anneal at 300 °C for 3 days in an argon atmosphere of 99.99% purity — one of a series of 300 °C anneals of different durations on the same Fe-16%Al monocrystal, chosen to set an intermediate degree of atomic order. In the wider study, short anneals up to 300 °C were always performed in high-purity argon, whereas all higher-temperature treatments used specimens encapsulated in evacuated (10⁻⁶ bar) SiO2 ampoules.
microstructure: The specimen is a monocrystal of Fe-16%Al with no grain boundaries; the pieces studied for hardness were (111)-oriented. Its constitution is an Fe–Al solid solution in the K-state regime, characterised by short-range ordering of still unclear character rather than by long-range order; after the 300 °C/3 day anneal the degree of short-range order is intermediate (maximum ordering in the series is reached by a 250 °C/14 day anneal, minimum by quenching from 1100 or 600 °C). The only second phase present is rare globular AlN inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm, identified by EDX. No carbides were detected in this monocrystal, which contains 45 wt.ppm C — consistent with the observation that thin plate- or rod-like carbides in the alloys appear only on grain boundaries after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or prolonged annealing, and were found in the Fe-16%Al monocrystal after a 320 °C/14 day treatment only when that heat treatment was combined with 100 MPa loading in the <111> direction.
properties: Mechanical response was probed by room-temperature universal hardness (HU) on a Fischerscope H100 microhardness tester with a maximum load of 1 N, with HU defined as F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²] and reported values averaged over more than 40 measurements. The 300 °C/3 day-annealed monocrystal gives HU ≈ 2000 N/mm², identical to the as-grown monocrystal. Across the whole heat-treatment series of this Fe-16%Al monocrystal, HU varies by only about 10% at most, the lowest values belonging to longer or higher-temperature anneals (e.g. 300 °C/14 d, 320 °C/233 d, 600 °C/6 h, 400 °C/6 h) and the highest to quenching from 1100 °C (with or without subsequent annealing). No tensile, compressive, fracture-toughness, fatigue or creep data are reported specifically for this annealed monocrystal, and no physical, chemical, radiation or magnetic property measurements are given for it. The characterization techniques applied to the object comprise microhardness/universal hardness testing and SEM-based EDX for the identification of AlN inclusions.
mechanisms: Annealing the Fe-16%Al monocrystal at 300 °C for 3 days sets an intermediate degree of short-range order (the K-state), yet the resulting HU ≈ 2000 N/mm² equals that of the as-grown crystal; because maximum ordering (250 °C/14 d) and minimum ordering (quench from 600 or 1100 °C) also give the same hardness, the paper concludes that short-range ordering has no major impact on hardness.

Short-range ordering in Fe-Al alloys is controlled by heat treatments below 600 °C; consequently only heat treatments above 600 °C — not the 300 °C anneals — affect the mechanical behaviour of Fe-Al alloys significantly.

Excess vacancies quenched in from high temperature harden the alloy by acting as immobile obstacles to dislocation movement at low temperature, which is why quenching from 1100 °C, and not the 300 °C anneal itself, produces the highest hardness in the series.

Softening by annealing below the quench temperature relies on the healing-out of excess vacancies, which is controlled by a comparatively high vacancy migration enthalpy and hence proceeds slowly; the equilibration is so slow that even a 300 °C anneal for as long as 14 days may not fully eliminate the excess vacancies, which explains the only slight hardness reduction of quenched specimens after 300 °C annealing.

The linear increase of yield stress with Al content up to 18 at.% is produced exclusively by solid-solution hardening, described by Suzuki's theory of solid-solution hardening for bcc alloys; the measured hardening coefficient for the polycrystalline series is about 2.2 GPa, insensitive to deformation rate and temperature.

The decrease of ductility with increasing Al content results from a decreasing dislocation mobility, which falls as Al content rises and is further reduced by quenched-in excess vacancies; TEM shows that distinct dislocation cell formation (requiring sufficient mobility) occurs in furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al but not in the higher-Al or quenched states.

A reduced mobility of screw dislocations is a prerequisite for twin formation in bcc crystals and can be achieved by substitutional alloying and decreasing temperature; this underlies the deformation twinning observed at −100 °C for Al contents of 11–18% and at room temperature only for Fe-18%Al.
conclusions: For this Fe-16%Al monocrystal, the 300 °C/3 day anneal yields a hardness (HU ≈ 2000 N/mm²) that is the same as that of the as-grown material, and the whole heat-treatment series changes hardness by at most about 10%. This specimen therefore supports the paper's central conclusion that short-range ordering in iron-rich Fe-Al alloys, which is governed by heat treatments below 600 °C, has no major impact on the deformation behaviour; only treatments above 600 °C matter significantly. The wider study concludes that the room-temperature yield stress of the alloys increases linearly with Al content up to 18 at.% as described by Suzuki's solid-solution-hardening theory, that ductility decreases correspondingly with a ductile-to-brittle transition between about 15–18 at.% Al at room temperature (12–14 at.% Al at −100 °C), that low-temperature yield stress drops arise from the interaction of mobile dislocations with vacancies, and that deformation twinning at low temperature occurs because of insufficient dislocation mobility — the more readily the lower the temperature and the higher the Al content. The present results also contrast with an earlier report of a 25% yield-stress increase in a quenched Fe-16.5%Al alloy after a 1 h anneal at 300 °C, a discrepancy ascribed to differences in alloy preparation and impurity content.
unmapped: Placement of this specimen within the ordering series: the various heat treatments of the Fe-16%Al monocrystal give different states of short-range order — maximum ordering after the 250 °C/14 day anneal, minimum ordering after quenching from 1100 or 600 °C, and intermediate degrees of order for the other treatments — so this 300 °C/3 day anneal corresponds to an intermediate degree of order.

The excess vacancies relevant to the hardening discussion are introduced by quenching, not by the 300 °C anneal itself; the compaction/healing of these quenched-in vacancies at 300 °C is slow and may not be complete even after 14 days.

The hardness specimens of this monocrystal were the same (111)-oriented pieces studied separately with respect to possible ordering reactions, and the compressive stress-strain behaviour of the Fe-16%Al monocrystal (shown for the [112] orientation) likewise indicates only small effects of prior heat treatment.
